How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (Appellant), a citizen of Nepal, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated February 5, 2019, rejecting his claim for refugee protection on the basis that the Appellant failed to prove that adequate state protection is not available, and because there is an available internal flight alternative (IFA) for the Appellant in Chitwan. He alleges that he fears persecution and harm due to his political opinion at the hands of the Communist Party of Nepal Maoists (Biplav) (referred to herein as the Biplav Maoists or the Biplav/Chand Maoists) and its affiliated labour union cadres. He argues that the RPD erred, and asks the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to substitute a positive determination or remit the matter to the RPD for redetermination.
I allow the appeal and refer the matter back to the RPD for redetermination because I find that the RPD erred in its state protection and IFA findings. BACKGROUND Appellant's allegations

The Appellant is a (now) XXXX-year-old from Nepal. He alleges that he and his family suffered hardship at the hands of Maoists during and following the civil war that occurred in Nepal from 1996 to 2006 and during the 2008 election campaign. He alleges that, in 2011, the Maoist-affiliated Young Communist League (YCL) demanded that he quit the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX of the Nepali Congress Party (NCP) and join the YCL, or face harsh consequences. The Appellant, at the urging of his family, moved to Kathmandu in XXXX 2011 to avoid unpleasant consequences in the village where he lived and for further studies. In Kathmandu, he worked at a local XXXX XXXX, and joined a workers' union which he describes as a sister organization of the NCP. In 2012, a local leader of the newly created Biplav Maoists, a breakaway Maoist faction who opposed and boycotted the upcoming 2013 national elections, threatened the Appellant with violence if he did not stop all his election-related activities on behalf of the NCP. The Appellant reported the matter to the police who arrested some Biplav cadres.

Issues took place beginning in 2012 between XXXX and the All Nepal Revolutionary Hotel and Restaurant Workers Union (ANR Union), which the Appellant describes as a "Maoist affiliated" trade union led by XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX asked the Appellant to support his union's demands, but the Appellant did not do so. In XXXX 2015, the XXXX XXXX shut down because of issues between XXXX and the ANR Union. The Appellant participated in efforts to reopen the XXXX XXXX which succeeded in XXXX 2015, but although most workers were called back to work, members of the ANR Union were not rehired. In XXXX 2015, XXXX expressed his dissatisfaction that the Appellant had not supported the ANR Union's position and blamed him for the damage to the Union's image because it had not achieved its objectives with XXXX XXXX XXXX asked the Appellant to quit his NCP-affiliated labour union and join and support the ANR Union, and asked the Appellant to make a financial donation to the ANR Union. When the Appellant refused, XXXX threatened that he would pay a heavy price for his refusal. The Appellant reported the matter to the police, who regarded it as a political war between trade unions, and "did not take cognizance of" the report.

On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2016, the Appellant was attacked and beaten by six people, one of whom was XXXX. The Appellant was taken to hospital where he remained for four days. He was interviewed by the police, who took his statement in which he provided the details about the incident. The police informed him that they arrested "a couple" of persons involved in the attack. The Appellant stopped going to work and "was looking for opportunities abroad." In XXXX-XXXX 2016, he was granted a Canadian work permit as an XXXX XXXX, but was told not to go to Canada until XXXX. He relocated and kept a low profile. XXXX called him again, demanding that he withdraw the police complaint and said that he would not leave the Appellant alone until he fulfilled their demands. He received reports that XXXX and his allies were looking for him and he received a letter from the ANR Union (signed by XXXX) asking the Appellant to comply with his demands immediately. The Appellant travelled to Canada in XXXX 2016. His job in Canada did not materialize. He remained in Canada, but when his work permit was about to expire in XXXX 2018, he applied for refugee protection in XXXX 2018. He alleges that the ANR Union is still looking for him, and that a "group of Maoists/YCL cadres visited...[his]...home in the village several times...[and they]...tortured and threatened...[his]...parents to disclose...[his]...whereabouts time and again."1 His parents left the village in XXXX 2017 and are now living in Chitwan with his wife "because of fear of the Maoists/YCL cadres in the village." He alleges that, if he returns to Nepal, he will be beaten, tortured, abducted, or killed by the Maoists/YCL cadres. RPD's findings and Appellant's arguments

The RPD found that the Appellant was not a credible witness, and that his delay in claiming protection sooner in Canada undermined his alleged subjective fear, but the RPD did not decide the claim on the issues of credibility or delay. Instead, it found that the Appellant did not provide clear and convincing evidence to rebut the presumption that adequate state protection was available for the Appellant in Nepal, and found, as an alternative, that a viable IFA was available for the Appellant in Chitwan. The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in its findings regarding credibility, delay, state protection and the availability of an IFA. NO NEW EVIDENCE IS ADMITTED AND NO HEARING CAN BE HELD

The Appellant submits as proposed new evidence: a. An affidavit of the Appellant, sworn on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019, including, as Exhibit "A" the consolidated list of documents from the RPD hearing; and b. Exhibit "B" to the affidavit, consisting of 18 newspaper articles (26 pages), all dated between February 7, 2019 and March 13, 2019, said, in the affidavit, to "demonstrate the recent atrocities of the Maoists' Biplav faction."

Subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act 2 (IRPA) provides that an appellant may present only new evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that they could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection. If the evidence meets one or more of these subsection 110(4) requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible, and relevant before I can accept it (the Singh/Raza requirements).3 If it is accepted, I must decide whether to hold an oral hearing, but subsection 110(6) of the IRPA provides that I may only hold an oral hearing where the accepted new evidence raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the person who is the subject of the appeal; and is central to the decision of the claim; and if accepted, justifies allowing or rejecting the claim. The Refugee Appeal Division Rules (RAD Rules) also provide that appellants must provide a written statement indicating whether they are relying on any new evidence, and whether they are requesting a hearing, and that their memorandum must include full and detailed submissions about how any new evidence meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) and how that evidence relates to the appellant. 4

The Appellant did not submit with the Appeal Record a written statement stating whether the Appellant seeks to rely upon new evidence or whether the Appellant seeks a hearing. His memorandum contains submissions regarding "evidences [sic] that the Appellant asks the RAD to admit as evidence under section 110(4)..." The memorandum then refers to "media, newspaper and other report [sic] with respect to the recent Maoist atrocities across the country that arose after the RPD hearing," and states that "[t]he additional evidences [sic] are enclosed as Exhibit B, which clearly contradicts the assertion of Board [sic] that IFA is available at the city of Chitwan due to the fact that Chitwan is a peaceful area and alleged persecutors will not find him."5 There are no submissions as to why "Maoist atrocities across the county" are relevant to the issues on this appeal, and there is no specific reference to any of the 18 submitted articles or portions of those articles, or to how any of those articles or parts thereof relate to the Appellant, or to the viability of Chitwan as an IFA. Rather, the approach of the Appellant seems to be that it is appropriate simply to submit a significant number of articles and leave it to the RAD to read through them and speculate why the Appellant asserts that they are or might be relevant and how they relate to the Appellant. As the federal Court has stated, the burden of establishing the admissibility of new evidence lies on the Appellant, necessitating full and detailed submissions on its admissibility and relevance.6 Failure to provide submissions or explanations as to admissibility required by the RAD Rules is a sufficient basis on its own to dismiss an application for admission of new evidence.7 While the Appellant's submission that the articles arose after the hearing can be taken to be a submission relating to section 110(4), there are no full and detailed submissions regarding the relevance of these articles.

As to the affidavit, other than identifying the exhibits, the affidavit consists of a repetition of the basis for and history of the Appellant's claim. It and the consolidated list of documents are not new evidence and are not admitted as such. In addition, my review of the articles submitted as new evidence does not reveal relevance to the determinative issues in this appeal. The articles mostly relate to attacks by Chand Maoists at various locations in Nepal, most of them at cell phone and other infrastructure installations. One article quotes the perpetrators as stating that the series of attacks on cell phone towers, one of which was in Chitwan, are not intended to target any member of the public. There is no evidence connecting the ANR Union or XXXX to the Chand Maoists and there is nothing suggesting that these attacks create a risk for the Appellant that is any different from risks faced by the public generally in Nepal, or that they make it objectively unreasonable or unduly harsh for the Appellant to relocate to Chitwan. They have no probative value or relevance to the determinative issues. For these reasons also, the proposed new evidence is not admitted.

Regarding an oral hearing, as noted previously, the Appellant did not provide the required written statement as to whether he requests an oral hearing. The Appellant's memorandum appears to argue that the RAD has discretion to decide whether to hold a hearing "to give fair and equitable representation to the Appellant based on the merit [sic]." However, as noted previously, no hearing may be held if no new evidence is admitted.8 Since no new evidence is admitted, no hearing may be held.
The determinative issues in this appeal are whether the Appellant has established that he does not have a viable IFA in Chitwan, and has established that adequate state protection is not available.
paragraphs.heading_before: ANALYSIS OF THE MERITS OF THE APPEAL

paragraphs.text: Following my own review of all the evidence, including the audio recording of the hearing, and considering the arguments of the Appellant, I find, for the reasons outlined below, that the RPD erred in its IFA and state protection findings. Since that finding is dispositive of the appeal, it is unnecessary for me to consider the arguments of the Appellant regarding other findings by the RPD. I am unable to substitute a decision, and I therefore remit the matter to the RPD for redetermination. IFA ANALYSIS IFA test

The jurisprudence establishes that there is a two-pronged test for the viability of a proposed IFA, being (1) serious risk of persecution or harm, and (2) reasonableness, in all the circumstances, for the Appellant to seek refuge in the proposed IFA. When the IFA issue is raised (as it was in this case), the onus of establishing both prongs of the test is on the Appellant. Further, jurisprudence establishes that there is a very high threshold for the second prong of the test, requiring actual and concrete evidence of the existence of conditions which would jeopardize the life or safety of the Appellant.

The Appellant argues that the RPD erred by determining that Chitwan is a viable IFA without making an analysis in accordance with existing jurisprudence. The RPD's Reasons are very brief and followed a short hearing with limited questioning. I agree that the RPD's Reasons do not specifically address the two prongs of the IFA test. I also note that, although Chitwan was named as a potential IFA at the hearing, and questions were asked by the RPD that relate to the IFA issue, no submissions were made by the Appellant's counsel at the hearing regarding the IFA issue, and specifically, counsel did not submit that Chitwan was not a viable IFA.
I find that the RPD failed to conduct a proper analysis of the viability of Chitwan as an IFA.

In relation to the first prong of the IFA test, in order to determine whether the Appellant is at serious risk of persecution or harm in the proposed IFA, it would first be necessary to determine the identity of the alleged agent(s) of persecution, and then determine whether there is a serious risk of persecution from those agents of persecution. The Appellant's narrative states, at paragraph 1, that he fears for his life in Nepal "from the Communist Party of Nepal - Maoists (Biplav) and its affiliated labour union cadres,"9 while he states in paragraph 25 of the narrative that he is at risk of harm "by the Maoists/YCL cadres."10 At the hearing, the Appellant testified that his fear is of the Maoists Biplav faction, and other factions related to Maoists, and he also stated that he fears XXXX and his organization. However, the testimony of the Appellant, both written and oral, most frequently uses the single term "Maoists" to refer to political parties, parties to the former insurgency, labour unions, and other organizations whose underlying ideologies are communist or Maoist. In so doing, he conflates all Maoist organizations, while the history of the country shows that, despite often similar names, the various Maoist organizations are not always the same and do not present the same risk.

The RPD's IFA findings are contained in two brief paragraphs and appear to be based on the conclusion that, since the Appellant's parents are now living in Chitwan and have not been found by XXXX XXXX XXXX would be unwilling or unable to locate him. There is no consideration of the other alleged agents of persecution. There is no analysis of the means and motivation of the alleged agents of persecution, other than XXXX, to locate the Appellant in Chitwan. The RPD did not conduct a meaningful examination or make findings regarding: the existence, if any, of any connection between XXXX and his union and the Biplav/ Chand Maoists and any evidence of same; the existence of any connection between XXXX and his union and other "Maoist" factions or parties; whether the Appellant alleges a fear of persecution or harm from other "Maoist" factions or parties, and identification of those specific alleged agents of persecution; inconsistencies in the Appellant's testimony and his omission to mention in his narrative allegations that XXXX is affiliated with the Biplav Maoists, and allegations that agents of persecution have attempted to contact the Appellant or his parents in Chitwan (as opposed to at their former village) after the Appellant left the country; why there is no corroborative evidence from the "neighbours" who are alleged to be the source of the Appellant's information (and his father's information) about ongoing attempts by agents of persecution to locate the Appellant or his parents. There is no proper analysis of the first prong of the IFA test. Because of the vagueness of the Appellant's testimony regarding his alleged agents of persecution, which was not explored or examined by the RPD, I am unable to determine whether there is an objectively well-founded fear of persecution or harm from them, and whether they have the means or motivation to locate him in the IFA location, and the RPD did not do so.

In relation to the second prong of the IFA test, the RPD conducted no questioning at the hearing about the reasonableness of the proposed IFA and made no findings regarding this issue. While the onus is on the Appellant to establish that the relocation to the IFA is unreasonable or unduly harsh, and while his counsel conducted no questioning and made no submissions about this issue at the hearing, in my view, there is insufficient evidence to support a finding regarding this issue that would be more than speculative, and this absence of evidence cannot be resolved simply by reliance upon the onus of proof.11 STATE PROTECTION

The RPD found that the Appellant failed to provide clear and convincing evidence to establish that the police in Nepal are unwilling or unable to provide him with adequate state protection. This finding is largely based on evidence that an investigation of the attack in XXXX 2016 had been initiated by the police and, according to a letter from the police that was submitted as evidence, that investigation remained open and active as of XXXX 2018. The RPD found that this demonstrated that the police made "serious efforts" to provide the Appellant with protection, were willing to do so, and continued to "search vigorously [and with] persistence" for the culprits. The RPD did not engage with the evidence that, although the Appellant had identified at least one of the participants in the 2016 attack against him to the police, the police released the arrested persons because they lacked solid evidence of their participation without asking the Appellant whether he could identify the arrested persons as participants in the attack. The RPD also did not engage with the country documentation indicating that police will often not investigate or will drop charges and investigations against politically connected persons because of politicization and corruption of the police and political interference.12 This evidence is capable of contradicting the RPD's finding that adequate state protection is demonstrated by the actions of the police. I do not agree with the Appellant's argument that, the fact that no one has been charged despite the passage of time, is necessarily indicative of a lack of adequate state protection; many crimes remain unsolved in all countries. However, the RPD erred by failing to engage with evidence that arguably contradicts its finding.

The RPD also erred by finding that the Appellant failed to avail himself of available state protection because he did not report the further threatening letter from XXXX and his union to the police. The RPD did not engage with the Appellant's assertion that he did not further communicate with the police because of fear of being out in public, and did not explore why other means of communication (such as telephone, mail, or reporting by someone acting on his behalf) about the letter to police were not used. Therefore, the evidence does not disclose whether the Appellant's failure to report further information to the police was unreasonable.

The RPD erred in its IFA and state protection findings. I am unable to substitute a decision in this case as I find that there are significant issues that are central to the claim that were not explored by the RPD. Because it did not conduct a fulsome examination of the issues at the hearing, and because its Reasons do not contain a fulsome analysis of the issues in this claim, the record does not contain the information necessary for me to independently determine whether a viable IFA exists in Chitwan, or whether adequate state protection is available. There are also credibility issues that were not explored by the RPD. These unexplored issues leave me unable to decide, without hearing evidence that was presented to the RPD, whether the PA has established, on a balance of probabilities, that he faces a well-founded fear of persecution or risk of section 97(1) harm.

The decision of the RPD is wrong in law and the RAD is unable to make a decision under paragraphs 111(1)(a) or (b) of the IRPA without hearing evidence that was presented to the RPD. The matter is referred back to the RPD for redetermination.

The appeal is allowed. Pursuant to section 111(1)(c) and 111(2) of the IRPA, I refer the matter back to the RPD for redetermination. (signed) N. Kaufman N.
